questions.q: What is the main risk of over-retention?
options: It increases breach exposure by keeping data around long after any legitimate need
It makes storage too cheap to justify
It automatically violates every retention schedule
It has no real downside since storage is inexpensive
questions.explain: Every extra year data sits in a system is another year it can be breached, must be secured, and may be subject to erasure requests — the exposure, not the storage cost, is the real risk.

A permanent retention period with no end date
A classification label applied only to financial data
A type of encryption key used for archived records
questions.explain: A legal hold overrides the normal retention schedule for specific data once litigation or investigation is reasonably anticipated, so it isn't deleted on its usual timeline.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is a 'trigger event' necessary in a retention schedule, not just a duration like 'seven years'?
options: Because a duration alone has no starting point, and different starting points produce very different deletion dates
Because regulators require retention periods to be stated in days, not years
Because trigger events are only relevant to encrypted data
Because without one, data can never legally be deleted
questions.explain: Seven years from record creation and seven years from relationship end are different dates for a long-tenured customer — the trigger event is what the duration counts from.

questions.q: What is 'disposition' in a retention schedule?
options: The action taken when the retention period ends — secure deletion, anonymization, or archival
The initial classification assigned to a new data category
The legal team's approval of a retention policy
The encryption algorithm applied to retained data
questions.explain: Disposition is what happens once the clock the trigger event started has run out: delete it securely, anonymize it, or move it to archive.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say retention sits downstream of classification?
options: Because you need to know what kind of data something is before you can set a sensible retention period for it
Because classification is only performed after data is deleted
Because retention periods are identical for every classification level
Because classification replaces the need for a retention schedule entirely
questions.explain: The same technical column can need very different retention treatment depending on whether it's classified as regulated financial data or routine marketing analytics — classification determines which rule applies.
